cases.abstract: A long context window specifies how much text a language model can accept, not how consistently it uses the evidence provided. We examine this distinction by changing the location of answer-bearing information while keeping the required answer fixed, and by separately adding distractors. The evaluation pairs multi-document question answering on 2,655 NaturalQuestions-Open queries with lookup of random key-value pairs, contrasting natural-language evidence use with a simpler matching operation. In question answering, the tested models generally answer more accurately when the relevant passage appears at the beginning or end of the context than in the middle; GPT-3.5-Turbo can perform worse than without documents. Standard and extended-context variants perform similarly when the same input fits both windows. Yet positional sensitivity is not uniform across tasks: Claude-1.3 variants achieve nearly perfect synthetic retrieval, and repeating the query before and after the data brings all tested models close to perfect lookup without correcting the question-answering pattern. Thus, neither window size nor successful exact retrieval establishes consistent use of answer evidence in the evaluated setting.
cases.methods: Reordering the documents tests position without changing which passage supplies the answer. For each of 2,655 NaturalQuestions-Open queries with a paragraph annotation, we combine that paragraph with Contriever-retrieved Wikipedia distractors screened to exclude annotated answers. Moving the relevant passage probes positional sensitivity; adding distractors creates contexts of 10, 20, or 30 documents. Greedy decoding is scored by whether an annotated answer appears in the output, with no-document and answer-document-only conditions providing reference points. A complementary task places the queried pair among 75, 140, or 300 random UUID key-value pairs, with 500 examples per size and the same output-inclusion criterion. Using random identifiers limits semantic confounds and makes this a simpler test of positional lookup. Finally, placing the query both before and after the data lets decoder-only models process the context with the query already available, testing whether this intervention helps lookup and question answering alike.
cases.results: Additional context can negate the benefit of supplying the answer passage. GPT-3.5-Turbo reaches 88.3% accuracy with that passage alone, yet in the worst tested 20- and 30-document configurations falls below its 56.1% no-document accuracy. Because the answer-bearing passage remains present, these conditions expose a failure to exploit available evidence rather than a lack of supplied information. The nearly overlapping positional curves of the standard and 16K variants on 10- and 20-document inputs that fit both windows also distinguish window capacity from effective use. Query placement then tests whether a successful lookup intervention resolves the broader problem. With 300 key-value pairs, repeating the query before and after the data raises GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K) from a worst-case 45.6% to perfect retrieval. The same change leaves the question-answering pattern largely intact, slightly reducing accuracy except when the relevant document is first. Improving exact matching therefore does not, in this evaluation, remove the difficulty of finding and using answer evidence.
cases.notes: Retained the original diagnostic priorities. The abstract's closing inference and the Results query-placement contrast distinguish lookup success from evidence use (Sections 3.2 and 4.2); the Methods explains how fixed-answer reordering tests position (Section 2.1). Extended-window comparisons are restricted to inputs fitting both versions. Accuracy means answer or target-value inclusion in the output, not exact response matching. Architecture hypotheses and the retriever-reader case study remain omitted.

cases.abstract: Supplying retrieved passages does not ensure that a language model selects relevant evidence or produces claims supported by its citations. Self-RAG integrates these decisions into generation by teaching a model to request retrieval and assess passage relevance, response support, and utility through reflection tokens. A critic trained on GPT-4 judgments inserts these tokens into instruction-output examples; the generator learns to produce them alongside text. During decoding, each retrieved passage yields a candidate sentence, and the generator's own reflection probabilities help rank those candidates. Evidence assessment thus affects which continuation is retained, rather than merely accompanying the response, while retrieval thresholds and scoring weights remain adjustable without retraining or an inference-time critic. Zero-shot evaluations of 7B and 13B models cover six tasks. On ASQA, with the same five supplied passages, the 13B model achieves citation precision of 70.3 versus 65.1 for retrieval-augmented ChatGPT, but lower citation recall, 71.3 versus 76.6. Increasing the support weight improves precision while lowering MAUVE fluency scores. Self-RAG therefore offers adjustable evidence-aware decoding, with gains in citation precision that do not imply better coverage, fluency, or complete grounding.
cases.methods: Relevance alone cannot establish whether a passage supports a generated claim, so Self-RAG evaluates relevance and support separately. A Llama 2 critic trained on GPT-4 judgments annotates instruction-output examples offline with retrieval and critique tokens. The generator learns to produce both response text and these judgments through next-token prediction, excluding retrieved passage text from the loss. When retrieval is triggered at inference, each passage conditions a candidate continuation for the next sentence. Segment-level beam search ranks candidates using generation probability plus weighted, normalized probabilities for relevance, support, and utility. A continuation based on a relevant passage can therefore receive a lower score if its claims are only partially supported. Evidence assessment changes which continuation is selected, rather than supplying feedback after selection. Adjusting the retrieval threshold or critique weights changes generation behavior without retraining or invoking the critic.
cases.results: On ASQA, higher citation precision does not coincide with stronger performance across the other reported objectives. Given the same five passages, Self-RAG 13B scores 70.3 in citation precision, which assesses whether generated claims are fully supported by cited evidence, versus 65.1 for retrieval-augmented ChatGPT. However, its citation recall is lower, 71.3 versus 76.6, as is answer correctness measured by str-em, 31.7 versus 40.7. This comparison supports an attribution advantage, not better long-form answering overall. A same-data comparison tests whether training examples alone explain the gains: Self-RAG 7B reaches 54.9% PopQA accuracy, counting gold-answer inclusion, versus 48.7% for Llama2-FT trained on the same instruction-output pairs and augmented with retrieval only at inference. The difference supports the combined training-and-decoding approach, without isolating reflection from retrieval-aware training. Customization further exposes its operating tradeoffs: increasing the support weight raises citation precision but lowers MAUVE, while retrieving less hurts PopQA accuracy more than PubHealth accuracy. These controls accommodate different priorities rather than improving every objective together.
cases.notes: Retained the initial emphasis on learned evidence assessment and inference-time control. The Methods connects separate relevance/support judgments to candidate selection (Section 3.3); Results links Table 2 to attribution and same-data claims, preserving lower ASQA recall and correctness. Main models use 150,000 pairs; the separate ablations use 50,000 pairs and 150 sampled ASQA instances. Customization findings come from the 7B analysis. Shared ASQA passages do not imply matched training budgets. The same-data comparison does not isolate reflection; reflection scores are not independent verification.
